t: 3428. Maximum and Minimum Sums of at Most Size K Subsequences
o: We must sum, over every subsequence of size 1..k, both its maximum and its minimum element, modulo 1e9+7. In example 1 every subsequence of [1,2,3] of size ≤ 2 contributes its min and max, totaling 24. With n up to 1e5 we cannot enumerate subsequences; instead we count, for each value, how many subsequences have it as the minimum and how many have it as the maximum. Since k ≤ 70, the binomial sums per element are short.
k: Sort the array; after sorting, whether an element is the min/max of a subsequence depends only on how many chosen companions lie to its left/right.
Element at sorted index i is the minimum iff all other chosen elements come from indices > i: C(n-1-i, j) ways for j = 0..k-1 extras.
Singleton subsequences are counted once as min and once as max — which is exactly what the problem asks.

a.i: Enumerate every subsequence with a bitmask and add its min and max. This makes the definition concrete but is O(2^n) and only usable for tiny n; it motivates the counting solution.
s: Collect chosen elements, add min and max to the answer.
a.t: O(2^n · n) — only feasible for very small n

a.i: Sort ascending. The element at index i is the minimum of a subsequence exactly when the other j members (0 ≤ j ≤ k-1) are chosen from the n-1-i larger elements: C(n-1-i, j) subsequences. Symmetrically it is the maximum in C(i, j) subsequences. Summing value × (both counts) over all i and j answers the problem in one pass.
s: Sort nums ascending and precompute factorials/inverse factorials up to n.
For each index i and extra-count j in [0, k-1], add nums[i] × (C(n-1-i, j) + C(i, j)).
a.t: O(n log n + n·k) — sorting plus k binomial terms per element

w: Always present the counting idea: 'how many subsequences have x as their min/max' is the standard contribution technique. Pitfalls: forgetting the singleton case (handled naturally since j = 0 gives C(·,0) = 1 for both roles), and doing modular division incorrectly — precompute inverse factorials. Follow-ups: what if k were up to n? Then you'd need prefix sums of binomials per row, still O(n log n) with sliding identities.
